item.title: Enhancing Transparency and Replicability in Entrepreneurship Research with Preregistrations, Registered Reports, and Registered Revisions
item.content:encoded:
Entrepreneurship research, like many social sciences, faces challenges related to publication bias, selective reporting, and limited replicability of findings. While transparency and open science initiatives have gained traction in psychology and other fields, entrepreneurship research has been slower to adopt preregistration and registered reports. This special issue seeks to advance entrepreneurship scholarship by promoting transparency, replicability, and rigorous methodology through preregistration, registered reports, and registered revisions.

We welcome submissions that demonstrate how preregistration, registered reports, and registered revisions can enhance entrepreneurship research quality. Studies using these methods to examine key entrepreneurship questions, as well as methodological papers discussing implementation challenges, best practices, and frameworks for adoption within the entrepreneurship community, are encouraged.

Potential topics

  • Preregistration of studies
  • Registered reports as a publication format
  • Registered revisions to address reviewer comments
  • Transparency in entrepreneurship research methodology
  • Replication studies in entrepreneurship
  • Open science practices in entrepreneurship
  • Research design and analysis plans
  • Managing researcher degrees of freedom
  • Reducing publication bias in entrepreneurship research
  • Challenges and best practices for implementing transparency methods

item.title: Replication and Reproducibility Studies
item.content:encoded:
This special issue seeks to advance management research through systematic examination of replication and reproducibility in the field. The management discipline faces significant challenges regarding the replicability and reproducibility of research findings, with concerns about publication bias, selective reporting, and methodological rigor. This special issue provides a platform for rigorous empirical work that directly tests and validates existing management theories and findings.

We welcome contributions that contribute to our understanding of which management theories and findings are robust and reproducible, and which require refinement or reconsideration. Both studies that successfully replicate previous findings and studies that fail to replicate are valuable contributions to the literature, as they help establish the boundary conditions of management knowledge.

This special issue aims to promote transparency, rigor, and open science practices in management research. We encourage authors to employ preregistration, share data and materials, and adopt other open science practices that enhance research quality and reproducibility.

Potential topics

  • Replication studies that test established management theories and findings
  • Direct replications of seminal management studies
  • Conceptual replications that extend findings to new contexts or populations
  • Meta-analyses and systematic reviews of management research
  • Studies examining the reproducibility of quantitative findings in management
  • Studies examining the reproducibility of qualitative findings in management
  • Investigations of methodological rigor and transparency in management research
  • Studies addressing publication bias and selective reporting in management
  • Research examining effect sizes and statistical power in management studies
  • Studies on open science practices and preregistration in management research

Timeline

  • June 30, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Registered Reports
item.content:encoded:
In cases in which results, whether present or not, may have important theoretical or practical implications, scholars are encouraged to submit a Registered Report. In this type of submission, authors submit the introduction, methods, measurement info, and analysis plan (but not the results) of a completed or planned study.

This abbreviated paper is then evaluated on the basis of the importance of the topic, the merit of the selected analytic approach, methodological rigor and quality, and potential for impacting down-the-road theorizing and/or practice/policy. As results are not included in the registered report, what was or is likely to be found has no bearing on the outcome of the evaluation. This is in line with the journal's willingness to publish papers reporting negligible or non-effects.

Potential topics

  • Empirical studies with important theoretical or practical implications
  • Research with rigorous methodological design
  • Studies reporting null or negligible effects
  • Organizational and management research

Timeline

  • January 1, 2025: Call for submissions opens
  • December 31, 2026: Submission deadline
